summary:
The Pancake Tortoise — named for its remarkably flat, flexible shell — spent its life wedged into the narrow rock crevices of East Africa's sun-baked outcrops, navigating the scrublands of Kenya, Tanzania, and Zambia with quiet persistence. Unlike other tortoises, it could actually run and climb, squeezing into rocky retreats with surprising agility. It was a creature perfectly shaped by its landscape, returning to the same sheltered cracks again and again.

That loyalty to place became its undoing. Collectors supplying the exotic pet trade learned to identify every suitable crevice, systematically emptying entire populations. Because this tortoise rarely strays far and replenishes slowly, recovery is nearly impossible once a site is stripped. Its numbers continue to fall — a small, ancient life undone by human appetite.
